Industry observers note that the Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

My 15-year-old and I are both substantial Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

Seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that notes “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

Sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this new classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

This sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

This is a latest brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

Both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

My 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that for the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

This brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that these I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles.

My kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell.

If your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity.

I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that my daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell.

Buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity.

These M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles.

The problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that for the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a massive gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles.

All my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity.

For years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a new driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles.

I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that for the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that my artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles.

For the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that this is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this organization has been really great for us. I also love that this comes in a sturdy carrying case and with a swatch card, which my daughter loves to fill out as soon as she gets a latest set. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that for the tween or teen who's obsessed with her dog (or everyone else's), this dog-themed earring set from Pip Pop Post is a super cute way to show it off. The earrings are made from hypoallergenic 18k gold-plated stainless steel with colorful enamel, and they're free of nickel, lead, and copper, so they're comfortable for sensitive ears. They use flat screw-back posts that stay put through sleep, sports, and school, and they're waterproof and sweat-proof, so she can wear them 24/7 without a second thought! — Katie Garrity.

Every year, we get the kids a holiday-themed puzzle from Mudpuppy. The quality is great, and the puzzles are challenging without being a nightmare. Many of them have foil details, which make them so pretty and fun. Especially as my kids get older and there are fewer traditional toys under the tree, having a puzzle to settle around on Christmas afternoon while we watch 'Miracle on 34th Street 'is a real crowd-pleaser. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that if you were a kid in the ‘90s like I was, you probably remember the absolute thrill of a fresh pack of Gelly Roll pens. Well, I’m happy to report they’re still just as magical for tweens and teens today! This 74-pen gift set from Sakura has every color imaginable, from metallics to bright neons, and I know my artsy teen is going to flip when they find it under the tree. The pens are perfect for doodling, coloring, junk journaling, or even just making handmade cards for friends (one of my teen’s favorite hobbies). And, yes, I’ll obviously be borrowing a few for my own desk. — Julie Sprankles.

The 25 Most Crucial Fatherhood Moments In the Past 25 Years

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 21st century has been the century of dads.
  • Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father.
  • Sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 21st century has been the century of dads. Never before has the idea of being a father become part of the national conversation, and never before have dads faced an onslaught of shifting mores and expectations.

Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father. Scratch that — it’s probably the best point in human history to be a dad.

Sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers. If you were parenting during the industrial revolution, let’s just say the whole child labor thing got a lot worse — and off your watch. And what of the booming ’40 and ’50s, those supposed halcyon days that are so often held on high? Don’t let false nostalgia fool you — the infant mortality rate alone tells a different story: It has dropped 85% since the Baby Boom.

It’s truly never been easier to raise a healthy and maybe even happy kid — and the past 25 years bear the fruits of this fact. From public policy shifts to pop culture moments, to an evolving conversation about the nature of masculinity, the past twenty-five years have been full of great moments for fatherhood.Here are twenty-five of our favorite moments so far this century, all of which highlight how the culture of being a dad has grown, changed, and been celebrated.

If you’re not a dad, it’s easy to assume that Jerry Seinfeld stopped being relevant in the 1990s. But, one of the wonderful things about the 21st-century Seinfeld, is seeing this venerable comedian turn into a Dad Comic. In his 2020 special 23 Hours to Kill, Seinfeld brilliantly compares parenting to keeping a baby alligator in your house.

Recent findings suggest that “You put it in your tub…and you feel the little…bitey…teeth. And then time passes, and you think — You know, I think we have to get this thing the hell out of here!”.

While it’s fair to say that the legacy of Bill Cosby has been tarnished, it is significant that the very first animated series to ever air on Nick at Nite is a now-defunct show called Fatherhood.

To be clear, Cosby wasn’t really in the show, and though it was based on one of his books called Fatherhood, this show was very much its own thing. It’s sort of hard to imagine an animated show called Fatherhood in 2025, but that doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be.

Industry observers note that for what it’s worth, Cosby isn’t the only person who has a book titled Fatherhood. The editors of Fatherly published one, too, back in 2021. And ours is almost as funny as the Nick at Nite cartoon.

We’re gonna have two mentions of the Star Trek franchise on this list, so get ready for that. But, honestly, in terms of fascinating pop culture moments around fatherhood, the J.J. Abrams-directed 2009 Star Trek reboot has to be discussed. First of all, the trailers for this movie really used this tagline: “This is not your father’s Star Trek.”.

In a recent development, the funny thing was, with that sh*t-eating grin, Chris Pine’s James T. Kirk was very much representative of an old-school take on Star Trek, a ton of action, punching, and one-liners. The movie was also literally about fathers and sons, and how people forge their own paths outside of the legacy they’re expected to carry. Plus, can you believe that a pre-Thor Chris Hemsworth played Chris Pine’s dad?

In a recent development, today, George Lucas has four kids in total, but during the era of the Star Wars prequels, from 1999 to 2005, he had three: Amanda, Katie, and Jett. And all of them were in Star Wars. But, because Lucas is classy and didn’t want to make this into a major nepotism thing, those kids are all in fairly under-the-radar, secret roles.

Industry observers note that katie was even credited as “Jenna Green” for a background role in The Phantom Menace. Meanwhile, Jett plays a young padawan named “Zett Jukassa,” seen briefly in Revenge of the Sith. Finally, Amanda had a small background role in Revenge of the Sith, alongside her father.

Sources indicate that is being a father the way you see yourself? If you were a dad in the 20th century, the answer would be very different than it is today. According to a Pew Research Center survey published in 2023, 85 percent of fathers with kids under 18 claim that being a parent is either the most or one of the most “notable aspects of who they are as a person.”.

Sources indicate that this is huge. Identifying as a father first is simply something that wasn’t in vogue a few decades back. In the 1980s, comedies like Mr. Mom seemed edgy because of a challenge to gender norms. Now, those gender norms are utterly different.

Sources indicate that though the late Gene Hackman’s portrayal of patriarch Royal Tennenbaum gets a lot of the attention in The Royal Tenenbaums, this modern classic has another great dad role model. Yes, Ben Stiller is the man who gave us Zoolander, and at the moment, the mind behind Severance. But, in Wes Anderson’s modern classic, he also gave us a tender and hilarious portrayal of fatherhood.

Chas Tenenbaum is a widow, and as such, strives to be the ultimate parent, concerned with safety, and essentially begins the movie as a laughable helicopter parent. But by the end of the movie, Chas makes peace with his own dad, his demons, and learns to lighten up a bit. We could all have a bit of this character’s desire for organization for our kids. And we could all learn to change, too.

People can disagree on various problems around youth sports, but one thing all dads know is true is simple: You’ve got to support your kids. And so, NBA legend Dwyane Wade’s support of his daughter, Zaya Wade, is an exceptional example of what it looks like when dads step up.

On February 25, 2023, at the 54th NAACP Image Awards, Wade made it clear that standing with Zaya, who is trans, was his duty as a father. “Zaya, as your father, all I’ve wanted to do was get it right,” he remarked. “I admire how you’ve handled the ignorance in our world ... that you face every day. To say that your village is proud of you is an understatement. Thank you for showing me that there’s more than just one way to communicate effectively.”.

Industry observers note that the fact that Eminem sings a track rather than raps would be a significant cultural moment. But, Eminem’s “Hailie’s Song” in 2002 was a bigger deal than perhaps we’ve admitted. Prior to “Hailie’s Song” the image of Eminem was a little less sympathetic, but the utterly honest sentiment of the song for his daughter changed all that.

Industry observers note that it’s a song about a parent trying to explain the conflicting emotions inside all of us. Whether or not Eminem is a great dad or not isn’t the point. This song was a big deal.

Industry observers note that go to a party and talk to a dad about what they’re reading. At least half the time, if you mention Lee Child’s Jack Reacher books, you’re going to get a significant smile. Boomer dads love Reacher. GenX dads love Reacher. Millennial dads love Reacher. Currently, the Amazon Prime Video version of Reacher is one of the biggest shows on the planet, which makes sense since the fan base has been ready for this show since 1997.

But what’s significant about Reacher as a TV series is that it’s a vast improvement over the forgettable Tom Cruise movies Jack Reacher (2012) and Jack Reacher: Never Go Back (2016). Crusie was totally miscast as Reacher in those films, and as such, those flicks nearly ruined an excellent action franchise. Reacher is popular because he’s a vargant Sherlock Holmes fused with an American James Bond. Alan Ritchson’s take on the character has done what Cruise couldn’t do: Bring Reacher to the people.

Although Matthew McConaughey’s father passed away in 1992, he’s more recently come forward about how that death impacted him and his worldview. “Through the mourning and the pain, it’s the biggest moment of becoming a man.”McConaughey explained in a 2025 conversation with Interview. “There’s a certain safety net that I’ve always had behind me that’s gone.”.

Industry observers note that for many of us, McConaughey is like a Texan version of Yoda; he seems like he contains endless wisdom, and his approach toward life, love, and family is endlessly inspirational. And so, for him to be so clearly vulnerable about losing a parent is incredible. Losing a parent rewires your brain, regardless of age.

Recent findings suggest that there had never really been midnight releases for books until the year 2000. And this meant that the beginning of the century was kicked off with moms and dads driving their little witches and wizards to bookstores to get the latest Harry Potter books.

Industry observers note that while the first three books were very successful, the release of Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in the year 2000 created an utterly upcoming phenomenon. Many kids were driven to these midnight events by their parents, and a ton of those kids are parents now themselves.

We have a complicated relationship with Hogwarts and the Wizarding World these days, but for parents and kids, the Harry Potter midnight madness was a uniquely 21st-century event.

As soon as Mark Zuckerberg made Facebook available to the general public, the era of the chat room officially died, and the world of Facebook groups was born. Today, Facebook skews a bit older than some of the other social media platforms, and that’s probably because 19 years ago, contemporary dads were all still in their twenties.

According to recent reports, we got on Facebook back then, we created friend groups around different interests (Soccer, Video Games, Seinfeld memes), and now, we’re still there. Facebook groups didn’t start as Dad Groups, but that’s what time does to you.

LeVar Burton and Mica Burton, father and daughter, playing, father and daughter.

According to recent reports, if there’s anyone who really should have the title of America’s TV Dad, it’s LeVar Burton. Not only did he raise generations of readers on Reading Rainbow, thanks to his role as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation, but he also inspired countless people to tackle the STEM fields in newly introduced and innovative ways.

In 2023, Burton brought all of this metafictionally full circle. In the critically acclaimed Season 3 of Star Trek: Picard, Burton co-starred with his real-life daughter, Mica Burton, who played his onscreen daughter, Alandra La Forge. When those episodes aired, Fatherly talked to Burton about how Geordi was portrayed as a sweetly overprotective parent. Burton’s response was perfect: “I don’t know a dad who’s not overprotective. All dads are overprotective. I mean, we live in a culture and in a society where that is our primary responsibility, to protect, defend, and provide for. That’s why we’re here.”.

Today, it is well understood that The National is the most “dad rock” bands currently in existence on the planet. But this wasn’t always the case. There’s no way the band thought of themselves this way back in the early aughts, but something changed after the release of their 2010 masterpiece High Violet.

Sources indicate that without really meaning to, The National transitioned from being a really good band to the most vital rock band for a certain kind of 30-something and 40-something man. High Violet is the beginning of the version of The National we have now, and fifteen years later, we still owe money to the money, to the money that we owe.

When Robert Downey Jr. uttered the words “I am Iron Man” in 2008, it changed the game for male cinematic heroes. And so, it’s still hard to grasp that just eleven years later, in Avengers: Endgame, the heroic Tony Stark would die. But the most compelling thing about the journey of fatherhood across the saga of Iron Man wasn’t him defeating Thanos. Instead, it was Tony’s relationship with his daughter, Morgan Stark (Lexi Rabe).

As all dads know, sometimes kids come up with hilarious phrases to express their affection, and Lexi’s “I love you 3000” remains perfect because it’s so real.

In a recent development, one of the toughest afflictions that parents have to suffer in the modern age is the existence of a militia of mutant canines hellbent on providing alternative forms of law enforcement, healthcare, and basic public safety. We don’t know if the Paw Patrol is funded at all by taxpayer money, and we don’t want to know. (In the 2021 movie, we’re meant to think raw capitalism funds the Paw Patrol.).

In any case, Paw Patrol is a whole thing, and so, the moment in which Dax Shepard both embraced and mocked Paw Patrol in an ad for Paw Patrol was a perfect catharsis. Paw Patrol kind of sucks, but it also knows that it sucks.

In a recent development, paid paternity leave is more robust in the 2020s than it's ever been before. In fact, laws around giving employees paid paternity leave have only been strengthened in the past few years, not weakened. If you are a new dad and you’re wondering about taking time off in those early months, you shouldn’t really wonder. There’s a whole world of benefits for dads out there that simply weren’t as prevalent in the previous century.

No excuses, check out our guide to paid time off right here.

Daniel Craig’s 2021 swan song as James Bond wasn’t necessarily the best-loved 007 movie of all time, but it did deliver one of the best dad moments of the century. For decades, James Bond was a symbol beloved by dads, but a character who existed in a childless space.

According to recent reports, no Time To Die flipped the script on all of that, by revealing that 007 has a five-year-old daughter, Mathilde Swann (Lisa-Dorah Sonnet), whom Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux) has kept a secret. By the end of the movie, Bond has to die to make sure Madeleine and Mathilde can live. It would have been nice for Bond to live and be a family man, but as a symbol, the idea that 007 ends his life for his family was a powerful moment.

According to recent reports, regardless of how you feel about Bluey, the fact of the matter is that in terms of cartoon dads, the character of Bandit (voiced by David McCormack) has eclipsed all other cartoon dads. Not as overtly progressive as Daniel Tiger’s dad, but also not as horrible and useless as, say, Homer Simpson, the character of Bandit straddles the line between realism and aspiration with impressive nuance.

In a recent development, we may not all want to be Bandit at all times, but there is some version of various dads in him. Like it or not, this is the one that all future cartoon dads will be compared to.

When Professor Robert Kelly had a work call interrupted while on global news, a meme was born. He didn’t mean to become “BBC Dad,” but the hilarious moments in which his Kelly’s children waltzed into his work-from-home office touched a nerve with the parenting population of the world.

Ironically, just a few years later, after the lockdowns of 2020, many of us became BBC Dad, and in truth, many of us still are. The nice thing about BBC Dad, was that we could all agree that it was normal for your kids to exist right alongside your professional life. Things are messy, and you’re doing a lot of jobs at the same time. For many of us, it seems like our working hours never end, and that’s because, in truth, as a father, you’re never off the clock.

It has been revealed that prior to the 21st century, nobody needed to explain why J.R.R. Tolkien’s books were wonderful. And yet, in 2001, with the debut of Peter Jackson’s major screen adaptation The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, an entirely newly introduced pop culture vocabulary was codified. Fathers benefited from this because they either shared the films and the stories with their kids for the first time or were kids themselves when these films hit theaters. (Using Hobbit math, we’re counting being a teenager or being in your early 20s as a “kid” here.).

Industry observers note that for those who haven’t read Tolkien out loud to their kid, you’re missing out. And, it’s possible, without the popularity of The Lord of the Rings movies, several generations of parents wouldn’t have had the renewed permission to do so.

Of all 21st-century presidents, regardless of party or ideology, Barack Obama is easily the best symbol of a father figure who is as aspirational as he is relatable. As the dad of Sasha and Malia, Obama was present and also honest about his shortcomings.

It has been revealed that in 2021, Fatherly spoke to President Obama about how to find time to slow down and see your child grow up. He mentioned coaching Sasha’s basketball team, “even in the midst of the presidency.” He talked about the sheer “joy” of those moments, and regretted that he hadn’t “planned to have more of that” and a little “less of meetings in the situation room.”.

The reason this is so powerful is that Obama, like so many dads, admits when it gets it wrong. Having regrets and feeling like you wanted to be more present is part of the journey of fatherhood, and as a leader and example for other dads, Obama gets it.

In a recent development, whether you think about Bob Odenkirk as one part of Mr. Show, or maybe Saul from Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul, the truth is, the man is a national treasure. Brilliantly, he also showed parents everywhere how to be better at their most vital job.

In 2023, along with his daughter Erin (who provided the illustrations), Odenkirk released a collection of children’s poetry called Zilot. Here’s the thing: These poems were ones that Odenkirk wrote with his kids when they were much smaller. “I want to tell everyone, any parent who's thinking of trying this, and I hope you are, that I really did let the kids write the poems,” Odenkirk told Fatherly when the book was released. The result was not only a great book (seriously, quirky kids will love it) but also an important lesson to parents everywhere: Make things with your kids.

Recent findings suggest that during the age of the Baby Boomers, it was still possible to think of dads as distant, uninvolved people. Martin Amis described this phenomenon as being a “parent emeritus.” You’ve got the title. You’re hanging around. But what do you actually do?

According to recent reports, this attitude has shifted substantially in the 21st century. As of 2022, according to The Institute for Family Studies, college-educated fathers with children under age 18 at home now spend an average of 10 hours, 12 minutes a week on child care. Overall, the trend indicates that dads are 33 percent more involved with caregiving than they were in the previous century. Basically, the new generations of dads are nothing like the dads we grew up with. Which, hopefully, means the future will be even better.

26 Years Ago, One Underrated Nature Show Drove Kids Wild

📅 30 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let’s go back to the original Wild Kratts — Zoboomafoo.
  • It has been revealed that when Zoboomafoo premiered on PBS on January 25, 1999, families instantly fell in love with the high-energy Kratt brothers and the parade of live animals they interacted with during each 30-minute episode.
  • You and your kids might recognize its hosts from Wild Kratts, a popular PBS series now in its seventh season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s go back to the original Wild Kratts — Zoboomafoo.

It has been revealed that when Zoboomafoo premiered on PBS on January 25, 1999, families instantly fell in love with the high-energy Kratt brothers and the parade of live animals they interacted with during each 30-minute episode. Combining puppetry with real wildlife, its format was as unusual as some of the critters that walked, flew, and slithered across their set, and that’s what drew more eyes to the show.

You and your kids might recognize its hosts from Wild Kratts, a popular PBS series now in its seventh season. That’s the one where animated versions of the bros showcase the abilities of different animals, living a day in the life of that species while preventing bad guys from messing with the world. But the story of these zoologists begins not with flashy cartoons and super-powered animal costumes, but with a lemur puppet and his penchant for snacks.

It has been revealed that after graduating from college, Martin Kratt and his younger brother Chris traveled the world together making low-budget documentaries about animals for children. The handheld footage from these adventures became the basis of their first PBS show, Kratts’ Creatures. Aimed at preschoolers, the brothers espoused the uncanny abilities of the animal kingdom in a style that spoke to their young demographic.

Kids loved Kratts’ Creatures, and its success led the pair to a spin-off titled Zoboomafoo. Instead of sojourning across the globe, this studio show took place in a fictional reserve called “Animal Junction.” The brothers enthusiastically taught viewers about different animals with help from their co-host, a lemur who was the show's namesake. Whenever Zoboomafoo (Zoboo for short) had a snack, he burped and transformed into a speaking puppet who interacted with the Kratts and the episode’s special creature guests. A nature show for children like this was an untested and highly ambitious project, one that few believed would be popular, let alone become a reality.

Industry observers note that “A few production managers… during the planning phase quit because they didn’t think it could be done,” Chris said in an interview with Variety in 2021. “We had this puppet lemur that was going to sometimes be the real lemur and we were going to cut back and forth between them … It freaked out a lot of seasoned television professionals.”.

Undeterred, the Kratts made their risky vision come true, introducing home audiences to exotic creatures like the binturong or Kinkajous, creepy crawlers like tarantulas, beautiful birds like the kookaburra, and predators like wolves and tigers, assisted by the wise-cracking and curious lemur. There was even an episode about humans and what made them special within the animal kingdom. Whatever they were doing, it was working, as the ratings were phenomenal. It proved a hit among kids and adults, as analytics revealed high co-viewing numbers with families watching together.

The constant flow of animals on set meant production schedules were beholden to the critters, and not the humans filming them. The staff let the wild guests do their thing and kept the cameras rolling. It helped that the animals were usually babies, which typically made them easier to keep from getting into more serious mischief – even if that wasn’t always the case.

Chris and Martin Kratt chilling with their favorite lemur, Zoboomafoo.

Chris and Martin have been the face of kids’ wildlife shows for over two decades, but if you ask them who was the true star of Zoboomofoo, they’d answer it was the lemur. Two lemurs to be precise- one real and one hand-made - but both crucial to the show's success.

Gord Robertson was the voice and puppeteer for Zoboo, an experienced performer who worked on Jim Henson productions leading up to his time on the PBS Kids show. Robertson called it fun but “challenging,” often performing flat on his back on a concrete floor covered in mulch instead of the typical raised set he was used to. One thing that took some adjusting was working with the unpredictability of wild animals. Robertson was gassed by baby skunks, crushed by an elephant, and nearly mauled by a cougar (the same one seen in the opening credits), but the most harrowing misadventure nearly endangered the safety of more than just the staff on set.

“They had this bear who might have been a retired circus bear but he was a little skittish, and a bear is a bear- retired or not,” Robertson recalled in an interview from 2021. “I'm standing backstage [after they cleared the set of bystanders] and the lighting director is lying on a sofa looking at a monitor to watch the scene. We see the bear enter the shot, stand up, drop, turn, and run, and then he’s out of shot. All we hear is the clack-clack-clack of his claws running on the pavement!”.

After being warned by the animal wrangler to remain still, the bear sprinted past Robertson and towards freedom through an air conditioner vent. “He crushes the vent and then gets out of the building. Just as he does that, the trainer comes around the corner and states, ‘Where's the bear?’ I look at him and say ‘Outside.’ He says ‘Outside where? I say ‘Outside!’”.

According to recent reports, this could have been disastrous, as the studio was in the middle of a highly-populated suburban area in Toronto, Canada. Luckily, the bear didn’t wander far and was rapidly discovered back at his trailer. Production continued, likely with very few bathroom breaks needed by the human staff.

Caitlin O’Reilly, who helped build and wrangle puppet Zoboo, remembered the odd tasks she did to keep the faux lemur safe on the wildlife show, including “washing off camel spit, making sure the ostrich didn't poke at the puppet's shiny eyes, and ensuring the brave puppeteer didn't have spiders falling on to him while stuck in a barrel with his arm through a hole.”.

The real Zoboomafoo was just as adorable as his puppet counterpart.

It has been revealed that when he wasn’t a puppet, Zoboo was a real animal who enjoyed his time in the spotlight. Jovian, a five-year-old Coquerel’s sifaka lemur, loved leaping all over that set and hanging out with the Kratts. He grew up in the Duke Lemur Center in North Carolina, a sanctuary for these rare and endangered animals that Martin volunteered at while attending Duke University as a zoology student.

Industry observers note that from his soft creamy-white fur to his expressive face and bright eyes, it was impossible not to fall in love with Jovian. The young lemur was mesmerizing to watch, whether gracefully jumping across the room, climbing a ladder with his long tail following behind, or noisily chomping on a banana. "He'd jump in through the window and we'd feed him mangoes or garbanzo beans,” Martin recalled in an interview from 2014. “Sometimes he'd grab our noses with those soft sifaka hands.".

A second identical “Animal Junction” set was built in North Carolina to record the lemur scenes without moving them far from their habitat. Jovian, along with parents Nigel and Flavia, pranced and leaped on this set, using that footage for Zoboo throughout the series. Nigel and Flavia highlighted up simultaneously with their offspring during the episode “Happy Lemur Day,” an episode all about lemurs that celebrated Zoboo’s birthday, with his parents appearing alongside their famous ring-tailed son.

Jovian sadly passed away in 2004 at 20 years old, but his legacy continued with his other adorable family members, including children of his own.

While Zoboomafoo only lasted 65 episodes across two seasons, its presence helped elevate the Kratt brothers into the premier hosts for kids’ nature demonstrates. Today, Wild Kratts is one of the most popular cartoons on PBS, and a lucrative one as well with toys, books, and other products helping this show maintain its boa-constrictor grip on children’s entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that A Zoboomafoo reboot was announced in early 2020, but there have been zero updates four years later. While it’s been two decades since Zoboomafoo left the airwaves, there are still ways to watch it online or on physical media. It’s worth introducing it to your wild animals, especially if it makes them leap like a lemur to learn more about the wonders of nature.

This article was originally published on Jan. 25, 2024.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.
  • We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square.
  • In a recent development, over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

In a recent development, over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

It has been revealed that all teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

It has been revealed that when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

According to recent reports, not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

Recent findings suggest that by tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

Industry observers note that then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

According to recent reports, the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

Digital Detox Gift Guide: 27 Analog Gift Ideas For Lo-Fi Fun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.
  • We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits.
  • After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

Industry observers note that so this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

In a recent development, turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your latest one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

I have remarked for about 100 years that I wanted to get into embroidery. Whenever I see something embroidered at an antique mall or thrift store, I am enchanted, but... they are not cheap. Even thrifted! So, why not make my own? Clever Poppy is the perfect way to get an introduction to embroidery if you're a newbie like me. In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

There’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. You can’t skip songs, you can’t scroll... you actually listen to an album in its purest form. This record player makes that ritual easy, and it looks good doing it with its cool retro-inspired case and little viewing window. It plays both LPs and singles, and it’s compact enough to move wherever you want. I can’t wait to hit the local thrift stores and start building my vinyl collection. (Worth noting: This turntable does also have Bluetooth!) — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor of Lifestyle & Entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that for all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! I throw my book into my bag along with all my other crap and typically end up ruining it with crayon marks or crumbs from my kid's latest half-eaten snack. This protective padded sleeve keeps your current reads safe from crushed pages and bent covers (and mystery stains!). — Katie Garrity.

Coloring girlies, if you're not using Ohuhu markers, we need to talk! This 104-color pack is my go-to when I'm having a cozy coloring night with my daughter. Plus, these markers have a dual-tip marker design — choose the brush tip for sweeping, calligraphic strokes, or the fine tip for details. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve got nothing against my Notes app. In fact, I use it all the time. But I will always, always be a girlie who loves a really beautiful notebook and the way it makes me want to put down my phone and pick up a pen. This journal has a hard cover that comes in some really saturated, beautiful colors; I have the Mulberry and love it, but this Deep Indigo is next on my list! Little thoughtful details just make the notebook a joy to use: thick pages, a ribbon bookmark, a built-in pen holder, and a handy inner pocket. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, for the person on your list who has approximately 10,000 photos living in their phone and zero prints to show for it, a Mixbook photo book is the most meaningful and genuinely beautiful gift you can give. Mixbook is consistently rated one of the best photo book services for quality and customization, with hundreds of gorgeous themes and layouts that make the final product look intentional and special rather than just a dump of your camera roll. The design tool is incredibly easy to use, the printing quality is stunning, and they run sales constantly, which makes a truly luxurious gift very achievable. — Katie Garrity.

Anyone who has an addiction to making sourdough (or eating it like me) will absolutely love this bread bag from Keeki. It’s a beeswax-lined linen bag that stores your loaf and allows the bread to breathe. The natural antibacterial properties of beeswax will help deter mold! — Katie Garrity.

I’ve long been a fan of Papier, so I was pumped to see the brand venture into board games, starting with this gorgeous Midnight Mosaic Chess Set. It has a scalloped (!!) solid wood board with a full set of wooden pieces, plus a harlequin-patterned box pretty enough to live right on my coffee table. It’s more of a splurge than I’d normally spend on a board game, but I’m very into the idea of a set that lasts for years... something I can play with my kids now, that I hope they’ll ask to pull back out when they’re off at college and come home for a visit. — Julie Sprankles.

I wouldn't call myself an artist by any means, so that's why a paint-by-numbers kit is perfect. I get the zen of coloring, but the end product is pre-made to be gorgeous! — Katie Garrity.

For the book lover who’s trying to put down the phone, this is Chutes and Ladders with a literary twist, played on a gorgeous bookshelf board illustrated by Hyesu Lee, where ladders send you up and bookmark ribbons slide you back down (instead of snakes). It’s easy enough for little kids and charming enough for adults, with four wooden game pieces and two dice for 2 to 4 players, so it’s a great pick for family game night. It’s the kind of analog gift that actually gets pulled out and played, and it looks too pretty to hide in a closet! — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I am just now really getting into Pilates, and I feel like it’s such a top-tier analog activity. No screens, no notifications. Just me and my breath (and my very shaky core, ha). These Fraise socks make the practice a little more luxe! They have a non-slip grip that actually sticks, compression arch support, odor-resistant organic cotton, and a really cute aesthetic, too. But what I REALLY love is that this minority-woman-owned company donates a pair of socks to local women’s shelters for every order. — Julie Sprankles.

For the adult who needs a break from wrapping presents, this spiral-bound activity book is basically Highlights for Children, but with a lot more sarcasm and a festive attitude. It has 200 pages of hidden-picture puzzles, mazes, coloring pages, connect-the-dots, festive sudoku, and word searches, all printed on uncoated paper that’s great for pens or pencils, with an answer key in the back so no one has to suffer. It’s a screen-free, hilariously unproductive gift that makes a great stocking stuffer for anyone who needs a place to hide from the relatives! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that for the sports fanatic who already owns every jersey and mug, these books are a screen-free gift that relives their team’s biggest games, seasons, and championships through the real newspaper coverage printed at the time. They come in football, baseball, basketball, hockey, soccer, and more, and you can customize each one by choosing the cover color and design, adding their name to the front, and writing your own dedication inside. It’s an analog gift that feels personal and gets proudly displayed on the coffee table instead of shoved in a drawer! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that these Matryoshka measuring cups just make me smile! The design is whimsical and charming, but also super practical: Each cup in the set of six stands upright, nests neatly inside the next, and measures from 1/4 cup to a full cup. They’re great for spending time baking with the kids! — Julie Sprankles.

If you want to romanticize the analog life, this is the pen that does it, because writing with a solid 14K gold nib feels nothing like a regular pen, and the smoothness alone makes grocery lists feel like an entire event. The weighty metal body in matte black was designed by Mario Bellini and has a grooved texture that’s as satisfying to hold as it is to look at, and it comes with a converter and an ink cartridge so you can start writing right out of the box. It’s the kind of pen that gets you to slow down, pick up a notebook, and actually put thoughts on paper, which feels like the whole point of an analog gift guide! — Katie Garrity.

My idea of a perfect night is analog all the way: a puzzle on the table, no screens, and something truly cozy to curl up under. The stone-washed 100% cotton has that already-broken-in softness, and the tonal embroidered leaf design makes it look gorgeous without feeling fussy. It’s lightweight enough that you won’t overheat but still warm enough for a long puzzle session, and it comes with a quilt plus two matching shams to make the whole bed look put together. — Katie Garrity.

Nothing, and I repeat nothing, gets my family to put their phones down faster than the promise of melty marshmallows and chocolate atop graham cracker squares. I love that this Solo Stove S’mores Bundle makes real s’mores possible anywhere! It comes with a tabletop fire bowl, roasting sticks, fuel, and a bamboo tray to hold all the fixings, so you can set up your s’mores station anywhere from the kitchen counter to the coffee table for movie night. There’s even a fun little recipe book with creative riffs on the classic. — Julie Sprankles.

This is such a perfect gift for a music lover. You connect it to your phone and it displays the album cover of whatever song you're listening to. In a world where we aren't listening to music as thoughtfully as we used to, I love how this brings you back to the days when you would hold and see an album before you played it. This is the perfect gift for the millennial in your life who likes the way we used to do things. — Sarah Aswell.

Tried and true! You cannot go wrong with a good LEGO set, and this one is a classic in our house. I have it in a real vase on my desk, and it just looks so cute. — Katie Garrity.

There is something so nostalgic and special about instant cameras. There's such a sense of joy in seeing a photo printed out on photo paper instead of collecting digital dust in your phone's camera roll. Bring this as a hostess gift to your next event, and I promise, everyone will be fighting over it. — Katie Garrity.

These coloring books are so special for so many reasons. First, the manufacturer proudly donates 10% of all proceeds to animal rescue and rehabilitation efforts, helping more dogs find the love, safety, and second chances they deserve. Secondly, these images are based on the founder's own dogs! — Katie Garrity.

Welp, it’s finally happening: I’m late to the party, but I’m hopping on the mahjong train thanks to this limited-edition holiday set. Wildwonder teamed up with AAPI artist Joy Cho of Oh Joy, and her vibrant style really shines through here: The whole thing is stunning and cool and creative. Inside are 160 extra-thick, hand-painted tiles, plus dice and a Birdie Bam tile. Bonus: It comes with a six-pack of Wildwonder sparkling drinks, which are delish (the Mango Gold is my fave). — Julie Sprankles.

One of our favorite things to do as a family is family read-a-thons in the living room: We all grab a blanket and our favorite book. My daughter now begs me to bring out her adorable air mattress for a whimsical, super-cozy feel during our read-a-thons. It's even more magical under the Christmas tree lights! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking to get your kid off screens, the Yoto Player is our go-to. Our daughter absolutely loves hers. They have hundreds of cards to choose from (stories, music, etc.), plus radio stations and special podcasts. We have both sizes (we love the smaller Yoto for on-the-go), and prefer this over other screen-free media-type toys. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I didn’t get into bread baking during the pandemic, when it was all anyone talked about, but better late than never! I adore the idea of pulling a fresh-baked loaf of bread out of the oven, and I can’t think of a prettier way to do it than with this enameled cast-iron bread loaf oven. This dark red color is SO dreamy! I also like that you can use it for roasting recipes, and that it comes with a solid-wood trivet to rest on for easy oven-to-table serving. — Julie Sprankles.

The 100 Best Kids TV Highlights Of All Time

📅 30 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 74 min read (14732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~74 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From modern classics to the shows we parents grew up on, there’s never been a better time to be a kid with a clicker.
  • Industry observers note that today, parents probably spend more time not watching kids TV shows than actually sitting down and watching them.
  • Industry observers note that this isn’t to say children today watch too much TV, or that they watch more than we all did back in the ‘70, ‘80s, and ‘90s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From modern classics to the shows we parents grew up on, there’s never been a better time to be a kid with a clicker.

Industry observers note that today, parents probably spend more time not watching kids TV shows than actually sitting down and watching them. Unlike family movie night, children’s television serves one undeniable purpose in the life of a busy family: a virtual babysitter. And, unlike 30 years ago, thanks to streaming, children now can binge-watch, just like their parents, requesting “one more episode” sometimes sweetly, sometimes because they’re hooked.

Industry observers note that this isn’t to say children today watch too much TV, or that they watch more than we all did back in the ‘70, ‘80s, and ‘90s. And, in all the ways that count, what makes a good kids TV show is the same as it was back in the day: It’s a show that parents can walk away from, and, upon returning, won’t drive us too nuts. The greatest kids TV highlights of all time are those that enrich our children’s lives in ways that we can enjoy, too.

Sources indicate that here at Fatherly, figuring out which kids TV shows are actually the greatest of all time means embracing several of these paradoxes. The writers and editors of this list — all TV critics who happen to be dads — didn’t decide that all of these shows were the most educational, most popular, or most politically progressive for the moment we live in. Many of the shows on the list tick those boxes too, sure. But like film, TV is an art form that informs as much as it entertains.

In a recent development, these indicates are undeniably good — well-directed, acted, and produced — but they’re also, important. Great kids TV shows don’t just entertain our children. They inform them, subtly, or sometimes, hit them over the head with a message. They stick in the imagination of children, but not in an obnoxious way that is frustrating. Yes, many children’s shows are products, but the best ones don’t feel like pure consumption. There should always be something a little bit healthy in a great kids show, even if it’s just the fact that the show is extremely unique. Redeeming social value is good. Some educational value is great. But these things alone aren’t why adults watch TV, and this is also true of kids. So, we tried to think of not just great kids shows that are good for kids, but also great to watch. Some shows here are for very small kids. Some shows are for tweens. All of them are what we think are good shows first, and good kids shows, second.

Industry observers note that with all of those criteria in mind, we also aimed to have fun with this list. It’s not remotely objective, nor is it biased. Fatherly’s 100 Best Kids TV Demonstrates Of All Time, we hope, reflect the sensibilities of parents everywhere — it’s a little bit of this, a little bit of that, and a few substantial surprises along the way.

You may have heard that in the 2010s, My Little Pony rebooted and gained a following of a bunch of adult men who call them selves “Bronies.” While this phenomenon is notable, it does oddly overshadow the sheer brilliance, nuance and perfection that is My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic. Imagine a show where the comedy is so good, you’re actually looking forward to watching episodes with your little one. Now imagine that that same show has deep fantasy lore and interconnected canon that rewards you after you really get into it. That’s what Friendship is Magic is; it’s like Lord of the Rings meets Cheers, but for 7 year-olds. Some of the seasons beyond Season 6 start to push it a bit in terms of fresh ideas, but Seasons 1-5 are pure magic. For some Gen-Z kids out there, this show is already retro. But for your young ponies at home, it will feel brand new. — Ryan Britt.

My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic streams on Netflix and Tubi.

It has been revealed that from its opening theme song, complete with the word “fart” in the lyrics, Salute Your Shorts proudly declares itself as a show that is a bit sweet, a bit rude, and incredibly funny. Set at a fictional sleepaway camp, the show followed a group of a half-dozen or so campers (most with instantly-memorable names like Donkey Lips, Sponge, and Z.Z. Ziff) who were often at odds with the head counselor, Kevin “Ug” Lee. Despite only running 24 episodes, the show still maintains a strong cult following. — Caseen Gaines.

Salute Your Shorts streams on Paramount+.

The funniest superhero show...ever?

It has been revealed that teen Titans Go! is a comedy triumph, one that weaponizes any knowledge the viewer might have of DC comics canon against them and ultimately has them in stitches. In an era where meta-awareness is increasingly a requirement for robust franchises, Teen Titans Go! knows how to have fun with comic book lore rather than be bogged down by it. It’s both a perfect entry point to the DC Universe for upcoming viewers just looking for a fun time and the ultimate endpoint. — James Grebey.

Teen Titans Go! streams on HBO Max.

Industry observers note that hilary Duff’s Disney Channel sitcom still appeals to countless teen girls as much as it did in 2001 as it does in 2023. Like Lizzie, Duff plays a typical teen trying to make her way through junior high school and life, which means contending with parents and siblings, mean girls, crushes, puberty, and homework.

It has been revealed that what sets Lizzie McGuire apart is its effervescent star, Duff, a terrific supporting cast (Lalaine and Adam Lamberg as Lizzie’s best friends and Hallie Todd and Robert Carradine as her parents), and the animated Lizzie who expressed the character’s relatable, often panicked, feelings, fears, and aspirations. — Ian Spelling.

Lizzie McGuire streams on Disney+.

More reveals should be about people sitting around singing. Really!

Recent findings suggest that airing on Newly introduced York’s WPIX for 12 seasons — from 1972 to 1984 — The Magic Garden lives up to its name, a show about people sitting in a magic garden playing music. Hosts Carole Demas and Paula Janis interact with the Chuckle Patch (giggling flowers), a Magic Tree, and a playful, peanut-loving squirrel named Sherlock (puppeteered and voiced by Cary Antebi). They also put on little shows, sparked by what they’d find when they opened the Story Box. Demas, Janis, and Antebi recently reunited for a few live 50th-anniversary performances and they’ve still got it. It’s one of the most unique kid’s shows of all time, and it very much holds up.

Industry observers note that demas and Janis are planning to produce an animated prequel focusing on young Carol and Paula becoming friends and discovering the wonders of the Magic Garden. — IS.

You can watch huge chunks of The Magic Garden on YouTube.

The bird really doesn’t want to be used as a record player needle — again.

Industry observers note that airing from 1960 to 1966, The Flintstones is basically a cartoon version of The Honeymooners, for better or for worse. Fred harrumphs and embarks on doomed schemes with his pal Barney, while Wilma and Betty look on incredulously. Add in loads of visual jokes and punny names — Ann Margrock, Stony Curtis, Mr. Slate, brontosaurus burgers — as well as Dino, the Flintstones’ pet pink dinosaur, who loves to lick Fred, and you’ve got a stone-cold classic. Late additions Pebbles, Bamm-Bamm, and the Great Gazoo actually improved the show. Does it make any sense? Nope! But the enduring brilliance of great kids highlights is that they’re sometimes not required to make any sense or be anything but entertaining. — IS.

The Flinstones streams on HBO Max.

The cave child is ready for a nap, please.

Ambitious way beyond its means, Sid & Marty Kroft’s Land of the Lost (1974-1976) sends the Marshall family — dad Rick, daughter Holly, and son Will — deep into the past (or something like it). There, the Marshalls encounter dinosaurs, and assorted creatures friendly (Cha-ka, a Pekuni) and dangerous (the hiss-worthy Sleestaks), as they struggle to survive and find a way home. Bona fide sci-fi talent — including huge writers like David Gerrold, Margaret Armen, Norman Spinrad, and Larry Niven — helped spin the show’s stories, particularly in its first — and best by far — season.

Industry observers note that this is one of those classic old family shows that is way better and way more sophisticated than some might remember, and ripe for revisiting. — IS.

Land of the Lost is streaming on Peacock.

Sources indicate that CBS ran Captain Kangaroo for 29 seasons, from 1955 to 1984, a remarkable, legendary run. Countless millions of kids — and then their kids — grew up with the titular Captain, played by the wonderful and grandfatherly Bob Keeshan, who also created the show. Episodes — many of which kicked off with a major celebrity greeting Keeshan with “Good morning, Captain!” — featured sweet stories, visits from friends, entertaining puppets, animated shorts, knock-knock jokes (followed by a cascade of falling ping pong balls), songs, birthday greetings, and more. Favorite characters included Mr. Green Jeans (Hugh Brannum), Grandfather Clock, Mr. Moose, and Dancing Bear; the latter three roles were all performed or voiced by Cosmo Allegretti. — IS.

Captain Kangaroo is streaming on the “Beta Max Channel” on Roku.

How do they afford the dog food?

It has been revealed that norman Bridwell’s beloved children’s books came to life from 2000 to 2003 as an adorable animated series (encompassing 66 episodes over two seasons) featuring John Ritter as the voice of Clifford, a massive 25-foot Labrador retriever. His owner, 8-year-old Emily Elizabeth, loves Clifford so, so, so, so much as a puppy that his size represents her love for him. And off on adventures they go, with Clifford’s size and puppy energy wreaking good-natured havoc.

It has been revealed that of all the Clifford adaptations, this series captures the heart of the books. It’s not so much about the problems Clifford creates. It’s all about Emily Elizabeth showing children what unconditional love looks like. — IS.

Clifford the Substantial Red Dog streams on PBS Kids.

Sources indicate that imagine a post-apocalyptic show, in the vein of Planet of the Apes, with a character who behaves like Arnold Schwarzenegger in the Conan movies. What you would have is the 1981 series Thundarr the Barbarian, which is shockingly good.

Sources indicate that some ‘80s and ‘90s kids like to say Thundercats was better. But the truth is, Thundarr is the true winner here, mostly because Hanna Barbera had the inspired gall to give Thundarr a knock-off lightsaber. – RB.

You can buy episodes of Thundarr on Amazon.
